title: Both mothers and fathers are older at childbirth.
subtitle: Australia · 1975–2024 · median ages for all births
caption: The two lines show median ages for mothers and fathers using a common starting year and age scale.
note: From 1975 to 2024, mothers’ median age rose from 25.8 to 32.1; fathers’ rose from 28.6 to 33.9. These medians cover all births, including later children.
takeaway: The timing shift is visible for both parents.
why: Compare the direction and size of change for mothers and fathers.
how: Lines; x = registration year, y = median age, colour = parent. Direct endpoint labels.

title: Childbirth has shifted into the thirties.
subtitle: Australia · 1924–2024 · annual age-specific rates
caption: Each column is one year; each row is a mother’s age group. Darker teal means a higher rate. The gold guide traces the highest-rate age group each year.
note: Rates include first and subsequent births. They describe each year’s population, rather than tracking the same women. Births below age 15 and above age 49 are included in the youngest and oldest groups respectively.
takeaway: Since 2000, ages 30–34 have had the highest rate in every year through 2024.
why: Reveal a two-dimensional age-by-year pattern across a century.
how: Rectangles; horizontal position = year, vertical position = age group, sequential colour = births per 1,000 women. Optional guide = highest-rate category each year.

title: Later generations completed smaller families.
subtitle: Women born 1905–1975 · completed fertility by age 49
caption: The horizontal axis is the mother’s birth year. Each point represents the average completed births for a cohort that has reached age 49.
note: The 1932 cohort averaged 3.10 births per woman; the 1975 cohort averaged 2.03. Cohorts born after 1975 are absent because they had not reached 49 by 2024.
takeaway: Completed fertility fell by about a third from the series peak to the latest completed cohort.
why: Compare completed fertility across actual birth cohorts, while distinguishing it from annual period fertility.
how: Line; x = mother’s birth year, y = completed births per woman. Direct peak and endpoint annotations.

title: Later births have not fully offset lower rates at younger ages.
subtitle: Five years · separate profiles · one common rate scale
caption: Each ridge shows birth rates across age groups in one year. All five profiles use the same height scale and have separate baselines. Dots are published age-group observations; hover over any dot to read its rate. The number above each peak gives that year’s highest age-specific rate.
note: The annual total fertility rate fell from 3.154 in 1964 to 1.481 in 2024. This is a period measure based on one year’s rates, while completed cohort fertility uses many years for one cohort. Ridges connect age-group rates and do not estimate a distribution of individual birth ages.
takeaway: The whole profile changed: rates at older ages rose from recent lows, while rates in the twenties fell.
why: Compare the shape and location of age-specific fertility profiles at selected dates.
how: Vertically separated area profiles with a shared height scale; x = age-group midpoint and height = births per 1,000 women. All observed points have tooltips, and peak rates are directly labelled.

title: The never-married population extends beyond the twenties.
subtitle: Census · selected year · people aged 15+
caption: Men are shown to the left and women to the right. Bar length represents the number of never-married people; the horizontal scale stays fixed when the Census year changes.
note: Among all people aged 30–34, the never-married share rose from 42.1% in 2011 to 49.5% in 2021. Never married is a legal marital status and includes people living in de facto partnerships. Counts also reflect population size and age structure.
takeaway: Legal marital status and current living arrangements answer different questions.
why: Compare the age-and-sex composition of never-married people and how that composition changes across Census snapshots.
how: Mirrored horizontal bars; y = age group, absolute x length = people count, side and colour = sex. Shared symmetric scale across years.

title: Partnership is increasingly separate from registered marriage.
subtitle: Census · selected year · current co-resident arrangements
caption: Column width represents the size of the age group. Segment height represents the status share within that group, so rectangle area represents people.
note: For ages 25–34, registered marriage fell from 40.6% in 2011 to 32.3% in 2021; de facto partnership rose from 19.3% to 24.5%. This table covers usual residents aged 15+ present in households, as defined by Census social marital status.
takeaway: Some of the shift from registered marriage is towards de facto partnership, while the unpartnered share also rises.
why: Show the joint distribution of age and co-resident partnership arrangement while retaining differences in age-group size.
how: Mosaic rectangles; width = age-group population, height = within-group status share, area = joint count. Consistent status colours across Census years.

title: Marriage and divorce rates have both eased.
subtitle: Australia · 2005–2025 · rates per 1,000 people aged 16+
caption: The two lines use the same population denominator. The shaded interval marks the COVID disruption to weddings and registration patterns.
note: Marriage rates moved from 6.9 to 5.3 per 1,000 people aged 16+ between 2005 and 2025; divorce rates moved from 3.3 to 2.2. Divorce processing in 2021 also affects interpretation. Dividing these annual counts does not estimate the probability that a marriage ends in divorce.
takeaway: The trend concerns the frequency of annual events; it does not follow individual marriages.
why: Place partnership changes in the context of annual marriage and divorce rates, accounting for visible disruptions.
how: Lines; x = year, y = rate per 1,000 people aged 16+, colour = event. Shaded COVID interval and direct endpoint labels.

title: Family size differs across parent arrangements.
subtitle: Census · selected year · families with dependent children
caption: Ribbons connect parent arrangement with the number of dependent children in the same Census year. Ribbon thickness is proportional to family count within the selected year; each year is rescaled to the same total height. The two ends have equal thickness.
note: In 2021, one dependent child accounted for 50.7% of one-parent families in this table, compared with 34.6% of registered-married couple families. Dependent children are under 15, or dependent full-time students aged 15–24. These ribbons describe a snapshot of families, not families moving between categories.
takeaway: Parent arrangement and family size are related dimensions of the family population.
why: Explore actual joint counts for two categorical variables and compare the joint structure across Census snapshots.
how: Ribbons and nodes; thickness is proportional to family count within each year, with the total rescaled to a common height. Left node = parent arrangement, right node = dependent-child count, colour = parent arrangement.

title: Change sits alongside continuity in family types.
subtitle: Census · selected year · six exclusive family categories
caption: Rectangle area represents family count. Labels give each category’s share of the published all-families total.
note: Couples without resident children rose from 37.8% of families in 2011 to 38.8% in 2021; couples with dependent children moved from 36.7% to 36.0%. Couples without resident children include both those before parenthood and those whose children have left home. Census confidentiality adjustments can cause small differences between components and totals.
takeaway: The dominant family categories remain similar, even as their shares shift.
why: Show the composition of the family population and its relative stability across three Census years.
how: Treemap rectangles; area = family count, colour = one of six exclusive family types. Year selection, percentage labels and full-name tooltips.

title: Living with parents has become more common.
subtitle: HILDA · 2001 and 2024 · weighted estimates
role: Additional; not relied on for advanced count
caption: Lines connect the percentage living with parents at two dates for three separate age groups. These are same-age comparisons, not individual leaving-home journeys.
note: Across ages 18–29, the share living with parents rose from 39.4% in 2001 to 49.9% in 2024: a reported increase of 10.5 percentage points. Published changes use unrounded values and can differ slightly from subtraction of the displayed endpoints.
takeaway: The parental home remains part of adult family life for a larger share of young people.
why: Compare the size and direction of endpoint changes across age groups, with an optional sex comparison.
how: Slopegraph lines and endpoints; x = survey year, y = living-with-parents percentage, colour = age group. Direct labels and sex selector.

title: Fertility declined across all 88 mapped regions.
subtitle: SA4 regions · three-year averages ending 2013 and 2024
caption: Darker teal means a larger fall in births per woman. Values compare the three-year averages ending in 2013 and 2024, using the same 2021 regional boundaries.
note: The falls range from 0.03 to 0.66 births per woman across the matched regions. Large land areas dominate a conventional map even when their populations are small.
takeaway: The decline is geographically widespread, with substantial variation in its size.
why: Show the spatial pattern of regional fertility change using rates rather than raw counts.
how: Choropleth polygons; sequential colour = magnitude of fertility decline. Australian conic equal-area projection, tooltips and a linked region highlight.

title: Birth counts and parent ages add a different view.
subtitle: SA4 regions · births in 2024 · mother-age change, 2011–2024
role: Map 2; not relied on for advanced count
caption: Circle area represents the number of registered births in 2024. Colour represents the increase in median mother age from 2011 to 2024. Symbols use official ABS regional map points.
note: Median mother age rose by 0.5 to 2.1 years across all mapped regions. The 88 matched regions contain 291,330 registered births in 2024; the national total of 292,318 also includes records outside this matched set. Medians concern all births.
takeaway: Counts describe the scale of births, while the colour reveals a change in their timing.
why: Combine the scale of births with change in parental age while making the two measures visually distinct.
how: Circles on an equal-area map; symbol area = 2024 births, sequential colour = mother-age increase. Separate legends and a linked region highlight.

title: A widespread shift, in the places people live.
subtitle: 2024 population · one dot ≈ 25,000 people · colour = fertility decline, 2013–2024
caption: Dots make population concentration visible within the actual SA4 boundaries. Each dot represents approximately 25,000 residents; colour shows the regional fertility decline. Hover over a dot or choose a region to read its figures.
note: Dot positions are illustrative placements within each region, not addresses or observed locations of individual people. Counts are rounded to the nearest dot. The 1,088 dots represent approximately 27.2 million people across the 88 mapped regions; the source population total is 27,189,375. Fertility values compare the three-year averages ending 2013 and 2024.
takeaway: Changing the geographic encoding changes which parts of the population attract attention, without changing the regional fertility values.
why: Show the population context of regional fertility decline while keeping regions in their actual geographic positions.
how: Uniform-size dots; one dot represents approximately 25,000 residents. Dot centres are sampled within the correct projected regional polygon. Colour represents fertility decline, and region selection links to the other maps.
